utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning, everybody. Mr. Brdjanin. Good morning to you. Could you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case number IT-99-36-T, the Prosecutor versus Radoslav Brdjanin and Momir Talic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Brdjanin, as usual I'm going to put -- to ask you whether you can hear me in a language that you can understand? THE ACCUSED BRDJANIN: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honour, yes, I can hear you and I understand you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. General Talic, good morning to you. The same question. Can you hear me in a language that you can understand? THE ACCUSED TALIC: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honour, do I understand you and I can hear you very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. Now, appearances for the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Your Honours, for the Prosecution, Anna Richterova, Joanna Korner and Denise Gustin, case manager.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning to you. For Mr. Brdjanin?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Morning, Your Honours I'm John Ackerman along with Tania Radosavljevic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ackerman. And for General Talic? MR. DE ROUX: [Interpretation] Xavier de Roux, attorney at law from Paris together with my co-counsel, Natasha Fauveau-Ivanovic. Mr. President, my client, General Talic, made me aware of his wish to change his Defence counsel. He doesn't seem to have enough confidence in my health, which I have to say it's not at its best at the moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: General Talic? THE ACCUSED TALIC: [Interpretation] Your Honours, my Defence counsel told me that for reasons of health, he is not in a position to attend the hearings as much as it would be desirable, as far as the Chamber is concerned, and I think that the quality of my Defence would be affected if my Defence counsel cannot attend the hearings always, and it is quite clear that it is of -- because of health reasons that Mr. de Roux cannot regularly attend the hearings. I am aware of the fact that I have to give up a very good and experienced lawyer, much to my regret. I should like to express my gratitude to Mr. de Roux here before the Chamber for the effort that he has so far made in my Defence, and also to thank him for leaving me as me Defence counsel, Madam Fauveau, who has so far participated in the proceedings in a very quality way and has successfully replaced Mr. de Roux when it was necessary. She will remain as my counsel until further notice. I haven't given much thought to my new legal representation. I was not -- I didn't have to and I wouldn't have to, had it not been for the health reasons that were explained to me by Mr. de Roux.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, you may sit down, General Talic. Ms. Korner?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think clearly this matter needs to be discussed in a little more detail. I was unaware this was going to happen this morning. What I would ask is, Mr. de Roux is here today, if we could complete the witness who is giving evidence at the moment, and then I think, Your Honours, we will have to take stock of the situation. Without having been taken somewhat by surprise, although not altogether I have to say, I don't know whether General Talic or Mr. de Roux have considered whether there is anyone else in his firm that may be able to deal with the matter, because otherwise, certain consequences arise which are not particularly happy to contemplate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Maitre de Roux? Thank you Ms. Korner. MR. DE ROUX: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I fully agree, but the wishes expressed by my client, it is evidence that the Prosecution should not have any concerns. My firm will take care of the legal representation of Mr. Talic for as long as Mr. Talic hasn't found a new Defence counsel. The dossier, the case file, will be transmitted without any interruption. I should like to make it clear here that I do not wish to disrupt the proceedings in any way. And I will see that no interruptions are made in any way personally.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Korner?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't think that's going to be particularly satisfactory because if General Talic -- if -- I'm sorry, if the firm, I think it's Gide Loyal or something like that, but I can't remember the exact name now, is no longer going to represent General Talic at all, then whoever is -- and General Talic effectively is saying he has withdrawn instructions from that firm, then whoever is going to take over will clearly need to become heavily -- well, I wouldn't say involved but will certainly need to have sufficient time to read his way into the papers. Your Honour, as I say, at the moment, I wonder if -- it may be that discussion between counsel when this witness is finished may be of some assistance, but certainly the rules, as I understand them would apply, was that if an accused person effectively is saying, "I no longer have confidence in the particular set of lawyers and wish to instruct new lawyers," then he is not really obtaining proper representation in any evidence that may be called, which can, of course, have an affect if there is an appeal. Your Honour, as I say at the moment --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We have to delve quite deep in this, and also --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: That's why I'm wondering whether it would be of some assistance if, as I say, at the moment, as I understand it, Mr. de Roux is here, the reason for the withdrawal of General Talic's instructions from Mr. de Roux is because of his health problem so that he can't guarantee to be here. So as I understand it, and perhaps we could confirm that with the general, he is happy to be represented by Mr. de Roux at this moment while he's here in which case we can certainly complete the witness, and then, as I say, it might be of assistance if counsel in this case were able to discuss the matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: General Talic, have you understood what the Prosecutor, Ms. Korner, has just stated? THE ACCUSED TALIC: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I understand the argument. However, I should like to advance an objection, if I may. I have utmost confidence in the firm of Mr. de Roux. That is not a problem. My main concern is the health of Mr. de Roux, and the fact that he can not attend the hearings as regularly as I would like and as regularly as you said it would be desirable. I think that next week, he is due to undergo some examinations and he will have to absent himself from the trial as early as next week. That was the main reason for my objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Usually, the problem, General Talic -- you may sit down because this might go on for a while and I don't want you to stay standing all the time. The problem arose not because Maitre de Roux had to absent himself for a number of sittings because of health reasons. The problem arose because his co-counsel, for the first 12 sittings, showed up for only two times. The whole idea of having a lead counsel and a co-counsel is not to have them always infallibly for each and every sitting here present. They can alternate, and most of the time they do. But that's why you have a lead counsel and that's why you have a co-counsel, but it's not tolerable that you can have a situation whereby both one and the other do not show up. In the case of Maitre de Roux, there was the full understanding of this Tribunal because health reasons take almost precedence over everything else that would happen to myself, it could happen to anyone here and if one is sick, one is sick. You can do nothing about it. But that's why there is a co-counsel. At the present moment, do you have a co-counsel because Maitre de Roux in a very responsible way when the matter was surfacing -- was -- when the circumstances were becoming what they were two weeks ago, he took the initiative of asking the Registrar of this Tribunal to appoint Madam Fauveau as co-counsel, and Madam Fauveau was appointed immediately co-counsel because all the documentation necessary was provided and the Registrar was satisfied with her qualifications and full ability to defend you. Something that Maitre Pitron had failed to do over a period of more than six months with the result that the Registrar was never put in the position of confirming him as a co-counsel. The Tribunal could not allow that situation to obtain because the Tribunal has a duty, has a responsibility to ensure that you are defended, that you have a legal representation, a valid legal representation, which you have now. Now you have a lead counsel and a co-counsel. If there is an assurance, and I don't know because maybe we may have hurried on your part the preoccupation of being defended by Maitre de Roux may have eclipsed all other considerations. If it is a question of having Mr. de Roux absent for the next week or so because of health reasons, the problem that was in existence two weeks ago is not in existence now, does not obtain now, because now there is a co-counsel. Two weeks ago, Madam Fauveau, I couldn't -- in spite of her great ability and capacity as a lawyer, I could not recognise her as co-counsel and therefore I had to go on the -- not on the attack, I'm sure that Maitre de Roux understands completely my approach -- but I would have been criticised, my two colleagues would have been criticised had we not taken prompt action to make sure you were adequately defended because at the time you had an unofficial co-counsel who was recognised as a co-counsel but not yet officialised, his appointment was not yet officialised because he had not furnished the documentation as yet, and you had a lead counsel who, for justified reasons, health reasons, could not be present. Had Mr. Pitron been present while Mr. de Roux was not, the Tribunal would have said nothing, because that's why you have a lead counsel and a co-counsel. And the situation now, as it is, if -- I don't know because when we talk of health, you never know what the situation is, and I will not even dare ask Maitre de Roux, but if the possibility is that, for example, we are talking of another week when he will be absent, provided I have the assurance that Madam Fauveau is now co-counsel will be here, I don't think that you should be concerned. If it's a question of Maitre de Roux telling us that, "I can't tell you what it's going to be like. I probably won't be able to make it for the next month, for the next two months, for the next three months," then obviously we will have to make a reassessment of the whole situation, always keeping in mind, however, that the situation is not now as it was a week ago when there was no co-counsel present, because now there is a co-counsel present. So of course, the Trial Chamber has no right to interfere in any of the decisions that you, General Talic, are entitled to take in your own interest and will certainly not try to tell you what to do and what not, but maybe I'm just suggesting to you to reconsider perhaps the position in the light of what I have just told you, and reserve your position until later, until more or less the situation, the position, has crystallised and has become more clear because if this is something temporary -- I mean a year ago this time, I was having some tests myself. I was worried for a week, I was worried for two weeks, I was worried even for the third week, I had things, we checked and we checked, but then it was over. So I don't know what the problem is but if perhaps Maitre de Roux's problem is just a temporary one, which could be -- which could last, I don't know, two weeks, three weeks, even a month, provided that he will be showing up on and off and you are always represented by Madam Fauveau, I would -- I don't know, perhaps, but I would like to suggest to you to reconsider the -- your position and perhaps reserve to come back to us on it and for the time being postpone or suspend your decision to lift Maitre de Roux of his responsibility as lead counsel. It's up to you, as I told you, the Trial Chamber will certainly not interfere with your decision or with what you believe to be in your best interest but I told -- I have said what I have said just in case you had not given thought to these possibilities or to these matters. I know that it's not -- I've worked as a Defence counsel for a few years in my careers and there were instances where -- when my clients were very angry at me, and there were instances when I made them very happy so I don't know. I'm making this as food for thought. I'm telling you this more or less as food for thought. If it's the case of thinking about it, having second thoughts about it, and then postponing your decision, perhaps you would like some more time to rediscuss the matter with Maitre de Roux and more or less he will be in a position to give you an idea of how long this is going to last or whether he himself could come up with some other suggestions. I don't know. Maitre de Roux is a very reasonable man. I have no reason to complain, and he understands why I went on the attack because I was trying to protect you in any case so I'm sure he understands that there was nothing personal between this Trial Chamber and him not being present. He had the full understanding of the Trial Chamber but we could do nothing because the co-counsel was not here. We would not have opened our mouth had the co-counsel been present. Do you want a few minutes? Maybe you could have another conversation with Maitre de Roux? Or are you firm in your decision and you don't want to discuss it any further?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I wonder if Your Honour would care -- I was hoping we could continue with the witness, but I think it may assist if Your Honours would rise for, say, 15 minutes while we all discuss the situation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Perhaps you could also, at least for today, at least for today, General Talic, at least for today, while Maitre de Roux is, still -- is here in any case, his presence is certainly not going to prejudice you, his presence today is certainly not going to prejudice you, it's his absence that could prejudice you, but his presence is of assistance to you and perhaps we could have your consent for at least for today or until Maitre de Roux is present here in The Hague, I don't know whether it was your intention to be here tomorrow as well. We could finish this witness and perhaps the next one. We have scheduled for this week.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, he won't finish the next witness. That's quite clear. Because we are not sitting Friday, we will be going into next week and he is a witness --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think I take up your suggestion which is an afterthought of mine as well. We will suspend the sitting for a quarter of an hour, if that is -- if you think this suspension can be of any utility, and perhaps you can have a word with Maitre de Roux, General Talic, and then we will be in a better position to know how to tackle this problem. Thank you. --- Break taken at 9.29 a.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The sun has come out. I hope we will get some good news.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour we are grateful for the time allowed. I think it's best if Mr. de Roux explains the position to you as it now stands.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Maitre de Roux, please. MR. DE ROUX: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I think that General Talic's position is naturally to continue with this hearing today and do the same tomorrow and to think, to reflect on the matter over the weekend with regard to his new position, but naturally, it is up to him to take the decision.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. General Talic, it's not that I doubt what Maitre de Roux has stated but we would like to have a confirmation, reconfirmation of this from you, please. THE ACCUSED TALIC: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I suggest that we continue working today and tomorrow in this way and I will think about the matter, but I insist that I would like to insist that Natasha Fauveau-Ivanovic continues to work as my Defence counsel until the end of the hearing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: What do you mean, the end of the hearing? Is it a question of a translation, interpretation, until the end of the hearing? Which hearing. THE ACCUSED TALIC: [Interpretation] Until the end of the proceedings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. THE ACCUSED TALIC: [Interpretation] The end of the end.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. You may sit down, General Talic, I thank you. Shall we admit the witness, Mr. Smailagic? Who is in charge that? In the meantime, General Talic, I mean, in an informal manner, I mean, may I invite you also to consider something very important, that it's in your interest that this trial, once it has started, continues, because if it has to stop and if, as a result, maybe your case will be separated from that of Mr. Brdjanin, you know what that means? It means that it will be another year and a half or two years before your case starts. Yes, Mr. Ackerman?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Before the witness comes in, Your Honour, may I just make a very brief statement? Just to give you experience, I went into the Celebici case at about this same stage, the case had already started. I went in as lead counsel. There was a co-counsel who had been there from the beginning, just like Madam Fauveau is from the beginning of this case. We had a two-week break. That give me time to read the transcripts and the pleadings in the case, and we went forward from that point. So if this situation is to cause a delay, I wouldn't think it would exceed more than that amount of time, which would not in my mind be grounds for any severance of Mr. Brdjanin's case, if that were the only extent of the delay. The longer this situation goes, of course, if we Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. wait for a month, then it takes longer for new counsel to get up to the -- up to date. If it appears inevitable that there is going to be a change, I think it should happen now rather than a month from now, because it just makes it more difficult as we get deeper into the case but that's just the benefits of my experience and take it for what it's worth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ackerman, but the question is whether Mr. -- Maitre de Roux's problem is a problem that ought to be considered or looked at on the long haul, in the long haul or in the short haul. I mean if it's something which will no longer be a problem in two weeks time or in a month's time, and Madam Fauveau now is co-counsel and has been active in these proceedings in the Pre-Trial as well as in the trial stage, I don't see why there should be a problem. So any way we will bring in the witness and we start with the witness, because this can go on and on. I'm sure that General Talic is a reasonable man. He will give what we have said his considered thought, all due consideration, and I'm sure that at the end of the day, we will find a solution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Before we start the interpreters, now it's 10.00, I don't know when you will require the break. Will you please let me know roughly about 20 minutes in advance that you would like a break so that we can organise ourselves accordingly? Thank you. Yes, good morning, Mr. Smailagic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The gentleman next to you will ask to you repeat the solemn declaration that you made yesterday.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You may sit down. Thank you. And we will be continuing with the cross -- with your cross-examination now from Mr. Ackerman, counsel for Radoslav Brdjanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: May I proceed, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, certainly, Mr. Ackerman, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I would like the Prosecutor to supply the witness with the statements that he had before him again yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Smailagic.

utterances.speaker: ZIJAHUDIN SMAILAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You now have before you, I believe, each of your statements, both in English and B/C/S, and I'd just like you to confirm that for the record, that you have them both there.

utterances.speaker: ZIJAHUDIN SMAILAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: On page 3 of the English version of your statement, I see the language regarding the change of names. You said, and you repeated it yesterday in your testimony, "I think they managed to influence a thousand Muslim men to change their names to Serbian names." And then you said, "A document showing this does exist, and I think I can obtain such a document from our archives." I have at least three questions regarding that statement. My first question is: Have you found the document you refer to in your statement?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAHUDIN SMAILAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't receive it. But the document does exist in Banja Luka in an institution. I can't say where.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: When you say "our archives," what archives is it your referring to?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAHUDIN SMAILAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sorry? We have the information for the men of Bosniak nationality who changed their names and other archives.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You say in the statement that you think you can obtain that document from "our archives." When you say, "our archives," whose archives are you talking about? What archives are you talking about?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAHUDIN SMAILAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm talking about our archives where we gathered information on the people who changed their names and where we had registered them.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And where are these archives?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAHUDIN SMAILAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't tell you. In Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Do you know where in Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAHUDIN SMAILAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And where would that be?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAHUDIN SMAILAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I couldn't say.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You couldn't say because you don't know?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAHUDIN SMAILAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, but for security reasons.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Why are there security reasons regarding your archives?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAHUDIN SMAILAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because of the fear that people who take account of these archives, who govern these archives, they could be maltreated, they could be misappropriated, destroyed, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Have you given the representatives of the Office of the Prosecutor access to these archives? Have they managed to look at them and go through them?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAHUDIN SMAILAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, they haven't.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Have they asked for access to them?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAHUDIN SMAILAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They asked if they could have access to them. I said I would try but that was -- I wasn't able to achieve this.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Who is the person who is responsible for maintaining this archive and who would have custody of these documents?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAHUDIN SMAILAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't tell you that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour I ask that the witness be required to give that answer. He can give it in private session if he wishes. I have no objection to that, but I think it's an area of investigation that I have an obligation to my client to pursue. There is law from this Tribunal that says that I must.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Ms. Korner?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, at the moment I'm not clear, I hear what Mr. Ackerman says, that it's an obligation to his client, but what's the relevance of archives showing people who have changed their names to this case?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ackerman? What's the relevance?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have the impression that the archives go beyond a list of people who changed their names, even if it doesn't. It is a document that the witness has indicated that he would obtain, which he has not done, and a document that I think would be important regarding, if it's just one document, which is not likely to be what one would describe as archives, that it is extremely relevant to the credibility of this witness. And the credibility of this witness is very important in this case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Korner?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: First of all, Your Honour, it sounds to me remarkably like a fishing expedition. There must be other things although we don't know what they are. Secondly, how can the existence of these archives be of relevance to the credibility of the witness?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The existence or otherwise of these archives may be relevant because if there are no archives and he is saying this document I can obtain, I can bring forward from the archives, and there are no archives, then obviously he's not saying -- telling the truth but the thing is that he is stating not on oath here, in solemnly declaring in his evidence, that there are such things, there is such a thing as these archives, that he is confirming again in his statement that this document exists, and that it is -- can be found in those archives. However, he doesn't want to tell us where these archives are kept in custody, and I don't think that I can see any relevance beyond that, and I will not insist on him giving information beyond that. We have established that he's confirmed here again that this document exists, that it is in those archives and that he wouldn't like to be forced to give further information on that because of security reasons. I will not insist with the witness any further.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I mean it's a question the credibility or otherwise is not going to be established by an in-depth investigation on whether these archives exist or not. If he is pleading a security issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour how could this witness plead a security issue? He's not a government. He's an individual. These are individual archives. What you're saying is that I am going to be deprived of the ability to investigate and properly represent my client when I find that there is valid area of investigation, it will be cut off.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Which valid area of investigation, that there are archives, that there is an archive? He's telling you that there is an archive. And he doesn't want to give you further information because of security reasons. Of course there may be security reasons.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Then there is a way to fashion a solution to the security reasons that would give me access to those documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Closed session, he will tell you that there is an archives but I will never reveal where they are and he will be protected in that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: The Tribunal could then order the witness to deliver those archives to the Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Are you in possession of those archives, Mr. Smailagic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Have you any control on those archives?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, because I live in Zenica and the archives are in Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: But he has stated that he knows who is in control of them and what I'm asking now is that he give the Tribunal that name so that I can then ask you to subpoena that person, to bring the archives to this Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I still don't see the relevance, Mr. Ackerman. The whole point resolves around the statement that he made here, that these archives do exist, that he knows that this document is in those archives. That should be enough. Whether we are going to believe him or not is another matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Would you then order him --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Taking into consideration that he doesn't want to reveal where these archives are and who is in charge of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: With you then order him to produce that document which he says that he can get from that archive?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Not if he hasn't got control over these archives any more.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm helpfully informed by Ms. Richterova who is the expert on these matters that there is a document in the Banja Luka collection referring it this change of name, which we've disclosed. So if the point started with "you've mentioned change of names," and that's all this point is about. In our submission it's tangentially relevant if at all to the main issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I frankly don't see the relevance except in so far as the credibility of the witness is concerned. There, I think, Mr. Ackerman has scored a point but beyond that, there is little if any relevance at all to the issue, because I don't think the question has ever been doubted as to some or more Muslim men or women in Banja Luka changed their name because they felt safer if they did that. That has been stated. Now, whether it's a thousand or whether it's less, it's not going to change the picture much. Yes, Mr. Ackerman?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: The point is this, Your Honour: It's not just this document. The statement --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: This is when Ms. Korner rightly, very rightly pointed to. This would not be turned into a fishing expedition.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I understand that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Do you think I'm going to open the door so that you will ask me to force the witness to give details on these archives before I first know what's going to be relevant and what's not?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It would be a fishing expedition.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, when the Prosecutor requested a subpoena to take all the documents from the Banja Luka municipality would I have succeeded in stopping that by saying it's a fishing expedition? It's an investigation and what I want to do is an investigation. It's not a fishing expedition. It these are archives. This witness has indicated it's not just one document, these are archives that his group collected and it's very likely that they are relevant to the issues in this case. If they are not, what's hurt? It's not a fishing expedition, it's an investigation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: This very likely is how can the Trial Chamber proceed on "it's very likely"? How -- what justifies you in stating that it is very likely? What do you know about these archives or these statements?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I only know what he said and you won't make him answer any further than what he said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: He referred to these archives only in relation to this document that purports to prove that there was about 1.000 Muslim men who changed the names from Muslim names to Serbian names. I mean that's -- in actual fact in his evidence yesterday he even said that in reality most of them were women rather than men. If I remember him saying, if I remember him correctly.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You're correct, Your Honour, that's what he said.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour in the Banja Luka binder, exhibited as P135, disclosure number 1.112, there is a long list of change of names, starting in all the municipalities beginning with Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Which?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours will find it in binder number 1, I think. I'm told yes. The number is Prosecution Exhibit 135.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I don't have binder number 1 here because I told my secretary to bring me only 2 and 3 because those were -- contained the documents that you were going to refer to or that we were going to refer to. So yes, Maitre de Roux? Yes, please. MR. DE ROUX: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I don't want to extend, prolong this exchange, but I think that the only question that is raised now is to know what these archives are, when he says, "Our archives," are they his personal archives? Are they the archives of the SDA? Are they the archives of a group that he belonged to? I think this is the only relevant question at the moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That is a very relevant question. Thank you, Mr. -- Maitre de Roux. I think I will direct that question straight to the witness who is kindly requested to answer it. What kind of archives are we talking about? Are these official archives of the Banja Luka municipality? Are these archives that were collected by someone specifically or by some organisation specifically? What are we talking about?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] These archives are the archives of the Party of Democratic Action.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And you want me to force him to bring them over, Mr. Ackerman? You still do?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: No, that's really the answer that I needed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. May I ask the Registrar to show the witness this document, please, and he will then be asked to confirm whether this is the document that he referred to in his statement or whether this is some other document? I would imagine that that is the public registry civil status official document, from the looks of it. It's not.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I had no access to this. I don't know about this document. But we had our information and citizens would come to us and they would tell us who had changed their names. They would tell us this themselves. They probably wanted to justify themselves before us. We never received from the MUP, the Ministry of the Interior in Banja Luka, information on people who had changed their names and we were in no position to ask this of them.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Just for Your Honour's information we have only translated parts of it because it's just a list of names

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. I thank you Ms. Korner. Mr. Ackerman I think I can call upon to you proceed with your next question.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: We are still on page 3, Mr. Smailagic, and at the bottom of that page, you mention a gentleman by the name of Muharem Krzic as the only SDA member who met with SDS board members after November, 1991. The first question I have is: Do you know Mr. Krzic well?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAHUDIN SMAILAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I know him very well. He was the president of the Party of Democratic Action in Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: When was the last time you talked with Mr. Krzic?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAHUDIN SMAILAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When did I speak to him for the last time?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: ZIJAHUDIN SMAILAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Do you mean in Banja Luka or --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: No, anywhere.

utterances.speaker: ZIJAHUDIN SMAILAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Banja Luka, towards the end of 1993, before he left Banja Luka. And I was with him on two occasions, in 2001, in 2001, in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And you have not spoken to him since you saw him in 2001 in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAHUDIN SMAILAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I haven't, because at the time I think he went to Washington, Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. to take up a post in the consulate. He went to work there, he was employed there. That is to say he still works there.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Have you had any conversations with him about testifying here at the Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAHUDIN SMAILAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. We never mentioned it. We had some other problems of a personal kind, because I was a refugee and this was also something, a matter that dominated our conversations.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Do you know Mr. Krzic well enough to tell us whether or not you believe him to be a truthful man?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAHUDIN SMAILAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I could say that this is something I can confirm at any time.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: That he is?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAHUDIN SMAILAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Didn't understand that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You can confirm that he is a truthful man. Is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAHUDIN SMAILAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That's what I knew him to be.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And if it is the case that Mr. Krzic made a statement to the OTP which he signed, in which he said that Radoslav Brdjanin was very frequently on the radio, TV, and in the newspapers, especially in 1993, before that, he was obviously not considered respectable as a spokesperson of the SDS, in 1991, and 1992, he was rarely interviewed -- if Mr. Krzic said that, that would be correct, would it not?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAHUDIN SMAILAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, if we are talking about spokesman, as far as I know he was never a spokesman of the SDS.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: The assertion is that in 1991 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Ackerman, I think I would invite you first to explain to the witness, if -- in case he doesn't know it, the difference between saying the truth and being precise.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, what we are quoting from here is a statement that was made by Mr. Krzic in writing that he signed, and what I'm mostly interested in in that statement is the one sentence referring to Mr. Brdjanin, "In 1991 and 1992, he was rarely interviewed," and my question is, just very simply, do you agree with that statement?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAHUDIN SMAILAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. He was -- that he was never interviewed? No.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Rarely interviewed, maybe the translation wasn't correct. Mr. Krzic says he was rarely interviewed. Not never.

utterances.speaker: ZIJAHUDIN SMAILAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. That's true. He wasn't constantly a guest.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You would accept the word "rarely," would you not?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAHUDIN SMAILAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Okay. On page 3 of your statement, and I don't know if it's the same page in the B/C/S version, I hope it is, you make the statement down toward the bottom of the English version at least, that the SDS was in charge of everything that was happening in the area. Military and the police were receiving their orders from the SDS.

utterances.speaker: ZIJAHUDIN SMAILAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Don't find that here. But it was like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And then you told the OTP investigator that you never saw any orders of that kind. So my question is: How do you know that the SDS was in charge of everything that was happening in the area?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAHUDIN SMAILAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, if it had control, if the SDS had control in the municipal staff and the regional one, the Regional Crisis Staff, then it's quite normal that they took the decisions.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right. You spoke to us yesterday of Dr. Vukic and I think you told us that Dr. Vukic was the president of the SDS in Banja Luka, correct?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAHUDIN SMAILAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And if it's correct, as you say, that Mr. Brdjanin was a member of the Banja Luka SDS, Mr. Vukic as president would have been Mr. Brdjanin's superior in the SDS hierarchy, correct?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAHUDIN SMAILAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he was his president.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I want to change to another subject now. In your original statement, what appears in English, and you acknowledged this yesterday, was that you told the investigator that Brdjanin's wife Perka formed an agency for immigration in Banja Luka. Right?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAHUDIN SMAILAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that's exactly what I wanted to correct when I saw the Bosnian text. I realised that it was a mistake, that I had been misinterpreted or maybe it was a typing error. I said that the woman that he saw frequently was the head of the agency, together with Mr. Glogovac and over the weekend when I had the opportunity to see the Bosnian version I made the correction. I think that I made two or three corrections altogether. It may have been misinterpretation or just error in typing.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: So your position is that you never took the position that this Perka person was Mr. Brdjanin's wife, correct?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAHUDIN SMAILAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, because I actually knew his wife.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: If you go to your second statement, Mr. Krzic -- the one from June and August of 2001, apparently the OTP brought this to your attention and so you cleared it up at that point by saying the following. This is on page 3 in the English version, about two-thirds of the way down. "I mentioned in my previous statement that Brdjanin's wife Perka formed an immigration agency in Banja Luka. In fact, I'm not sure that his wife is called Perka. What I do know is that his wife was involved in organising one of these agencies, although I don't know which one. I cannot recall her name nor can I remember who told me that." That's what you said the second time you were given an opportunity to talk about that, correct?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAHUDIN SMAILAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot exactly recall that, what I can tell you now is that while looking at the statement, I found this mistake and I drew their attention to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, have you found the part that I'm quoting from your second statement, where you talk about Brdjanin's wife Perka again?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAHUDIN SMAILAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just a moment. I cannot find it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: It's on the third page, it's actually the second actual page of your statement, the page 2 starts with, "Witness statement," at the top. If you turn over to the next page, you should find a paragraph that starts with, "I mentioned in my previous statement."

utterances.speaker: ZIJAHUDIN SMAILAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I found it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Would you go ahead and just read that to yourself and tell me when you've finished reading it?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAHUDIN SMAILAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This was taken after the first statement, when I spoke about Ms. Perka, I made a mistake there. You see, in Banja Luka, there was a story that went around that Perka with the help of his wife established this agency. I cannot confirm that. Those were just rumours, however this agency did exist and people knew about it. Everybody spoke about the fact that it was his agency, that is that the agency was under his control, and it was only logical that we should accept it as true at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: My question is: Is what you told the investigators the second time you had a chance to talk about Perka, did you tell them the truth the second time?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAHUDIN SMAILAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: So it's true that your position then is that Brdjanin's wife formed this agency and ran this agency, you just don't know what her name is, and it may not be Perka. Is that your position now?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAHUDIN SMAILAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but I did not have any document to base myself on. That was what I knew on the basis of the stories of my friends and relatives, when this agency was established, people said that there was this Perka who was involved there together with his wife and that formally speaking -- that formally speaking, they were in charge of this agency.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Do you now know as you sit here today who Perka is?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAHUDIN SMAILAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Frankly speaking, I really don't know much about her, I don't know any other details.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You told us that you know Mr. Brdjanin's wife. Do you know what her name is?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAHUDIN SMAILAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know her name, but I know where she worked, at the Kozara company, at the finance department, where I had a number of friends and acquaintances and I frequently visited the place.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: It's your position that she worked at the Kozara company; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAHUDIN SMAILAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Later, I think that she moved to the prison during the war, at least that's what I heard from a lady who used to work with her at the Kozara company.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have this problem that I need your guidance in how to deal with. I just received two -- they are actually photos, not photo copies, but photos of original documents that I got from Banja Luka that bear on this matter. All I have are what are photos of these originals, right now. I think maybe the first thing to do is just have the Trial Chamber look at them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Should we be discussing this in the presence of the witness, to start with?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I don't see any problem with that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But do you see any problems with that, Ms. Korner, not knowing what these documents are.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Exactly, Your Honour that's going to be my first.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I would suggest that the witness leaves the room for a moment, that he is kept outside at -- very much at hand, near at hand, while we discuss, see what kind of documents we have and then we will proceed with there.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: The other answer is Your Honour is of course I don't think he speaks English. Does he?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I don't take risks, Ms. Korner, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I had many clients in my life who told me they were illiterate and they didn't know how to sign and put their signature and then I came across documents signed by them. So Mr. Smailagic, please may I kindly ask to you leave this courtroom for a little while, for a few minutes, you will be called again very soon. In the meantime we have a short discussion on some documents that have arrived, which may have absolutely nothing to do with you. But we would like to discuss these in your absence. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ackerman? What are we talking about?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, these are documents that I received via email. They were colour scanned. I believe them to be original documents from official sources, that's what they were represented to me to be. I want the Trial Chamber just to look at them to see the official nature of them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Are they in B/C/S?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: They are.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: How do you -- I mean we were not quite sure whether the witness knows English or not but I can assure you that I don't know B/C/S. So can you at least tell me what kind of documents these are?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can we see them, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I want everyone to see them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Obviously, and everyone will see them, but in the meantime you can tell us what they are.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Just a moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Before I see them.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. Your Honour, will recall yesterday Mr. Ackerman complained when Ms. Richterova said that some -- the witness was going to refer to some documents, which had in fact been disclosed. Ms. Richterova -- or it was the day before yesterday, I think, simply we had omitted to tell the Defence we were going to be using them. Now, one of the points that has already been touched upon is this: There has been reciprocal discovery in this case. Mr. Ackerman has known for sometime that this witness was going to be giving evidence. Presumably he had instructions that there were documents from Banja Luka which the -- strangely enough, the Office of the Prosecutor in the view of the complaints that are made about the seizures, haven't seen, and we have not been given sight of this document in advance. Your Honour, I'm merely raising -- I don't want to go on doing this, but I'm raising this as a matter --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You are perfectly in order and I suppose Mr. Ackerman himself acknowledges that you are perfectly in order, but we will handle this regularly. First, I would invite you to inform the Trial Chamber and also the Prosecution what kind of documents they are, according to you, then we will of course see them, and then of course we will go through the usual procedure of having copies made and handed to the Prosecution, and if the Prosecution requires time to gather information on those documents, before you proceed with presumably questioning the witness on them, we will have to consider that. But obviously, mean, we are preempting several issues before we see what these documents are. Can you inform the Trial Chamber what documents you have just received from Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honours may have noticed that a few moments ago, the security guard handed my assistant here a couple of pieces of paper. That's what these are. I got them by email, I believe it was yesterday morning, along with some birthday wishes that came from Banja Luka for Mr. Brdjanin, whose birthday was yesterday. I can't read this so I had no idea what they were. I handed them to my co-counsel who then handed them to Mr. Brdjanin, and it was late yesterday evening that I learned actually what these were, that they were not part of his birthday documents but something else entirely. So I ask that they be brought back to court and I just got them back in my hands this very morning. I would have given copies to the Prosecutor, I do that regularly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We don't doubt that, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: If I had had them. And I can tell you what my understanding of them is. One of them is a marriage certificate which shows that Mr. Brdjanin is married to a woman named Mira and not Perka. And the other is a statement from the director of a company called Kameni Agregati which shows that Mr. Brdjanin's wife Mira has been steadily employed in that company since 1 July of 1980. And that's what I understand the documents to be, and I can hand them to the Prosecutor. I can do whatever you suggest I do with them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think the Prosecution can have a look at them even before the Trial Chamber does. And we'll have copies made. Do you require time, please? This is what the Trial Chamber would want to know from you, not necessarily immediately.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, even if these documents are what they say they are, and I have no reason to doubt that they are, and I'm not going to go into why if they were yesterday morning and Mr. Ackerman's co-counsel -- I'm merely raising this in the future because I don't want this to go on happening -- who can read this language and will have known from the moment she received them what they were, Your Honour, my concern is what is the purpose of putting them to the witness who will never have seen the documents before and inviting him to comment upon them? Now, Your Honour, I didn't interrupt Mr. Ackerman's cross-examination when he was putting things that Mr. Krzic said in his statement to this witness and effectively inviting a comment. It is not a proper way in our submission to cross-examine but I didn't want to interrupt.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I didn't stop him because you did not raise an objection.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I have a dislike of constant objections because I think it interrupts the proceedings and unless it's really vital I try not to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's very nice.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: But, Your Honour, this I do, now that we have stopped, Your Honour, all these witnesses -- these documents may or may not be genuine, and I have a recollection that when Mr. Brdjanin applied for bail, we heard about his wife and I have no reason to doubt this is correct. I cannot see the purpose of putting them to the witness and inviting him to comment on documents he couldn't have seen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: There may be a relevance, Ms. Korner, as I see it. It's again touch and go, but the Trial Chamber would rather favour being forthcoming rather than closing on the parties at this stage. The question is this or the problem is this: That you have the first statement where the witness stated categorically, Mr. Brdjanin's wife Perka formed this organisation, together with Glogovac or whatever. He eventually corrected that obviously because someone must have drawn his attention that they -- that may not have been correct. He corrected himself in the second statement.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, can I just, that's what was put to him and he was never asked if that was right. My understanding of the situation is that before the witness has seen it for the second time, the original statement is read back to him so we don't -- because he was never asked, we don't know whether he brought it to the investigator's attention or it was the other way around.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, he was asked yesterday. I asked him if the investigator brought to his attention matters from his prior statement that were not correct and he said yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's, yes. I remember him saying this. This is why I've just stated it. And then what he stated in the second statement is, first, that he knows Mr. Brdjanin's wife. Knows in a very generic sense. Secondly, that Perka is -- when he referred to Perka, he was not necessarily correct or precise because he is not in a position to confirm whether Mr. Brdjanin's wife is called Perka or not. And then he makes an affirmation that -- and now he in order to convince us that he knew who Mr. Brdjanin's wife was in his testimony this morning, he's gone beyond Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. what perhaps was necessary, telling us where she worked and where he obviously saw her, because he used to visit this place where he had many contacts. So I think from that point of view, given the circumstances, now that he has gone beyond what was actually needed of him, I would allow the question related as to the name. I don't think he is not going to confirm or deny that marriage certificate because he's not in a position, but at least the document itself should be allowed to be admitted in the records. Just to prove that Mr. Brdjanin's wife is not called Perka. Secondly, he wants to make a point that when Perka was mentioned as having organised this, couldn't have been possibly Mr. Brdjanin's wife. So that becomes relevant. The second point is to establish whether he could possibly be telling us the truth or whether he is inventing. It doesn't mean to say that this is going it prove that Mr. Smailagic is not saying the truth. Just as much as Mr. Smailagic's statement is not going to disprove or prove the authenticity of this document. I mean we are going to remain where we are at the end of the day but rather than taking the risk of not admitting questions and have problems later, I would rather admit the questions at this stage and play it safer. I mean, I think you understand what I mean, Ms. Korner, but I can read it in your eyes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, the proper question in my view -- in our submission, would be that the document -- if the document is to be put, having seen these documents, do you still adhere to your previous statement? But, Your Honour, I'm mindful of the fact that the rules here are not quite as strict and therefore --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: If you ask me whether we are wasting our time on this, I will tell you, yes, unless these documents will get us where Mr. Ackerman is trying to arrive, that is that this witness is not reliable. As far as that goes, yes, they may be relevant. Otherwise, they may be relevant only in establishing that this Perka, who organised this organisation, was not Mr. Brdjanin's wife, and if she wasn't, then maybe it's not correct to state that Mr. Brdjanin had anything to do with this immigration organisation. Still, I mean, basically we are going to get no where because the essence of Mr. Smailagic's testimony in this regard is that these were rumours and the Trial Chamber is not going it rely on rumours.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have nothing further to add on the matter. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, I think we can bring in the witness now.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour I think we need to mark them and I believe our next numbers are --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: That is correct? I think we are up to 44, aren't we?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I'm afraid I can't tell you whether you are correct or not because I'm not following the sequence myself. That is being taken care of for me by others. So I wouldn't know. Yes, please, bring in Mr. Smailagic.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The next number I have is 44.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: 44? We took it back? Okay. I will then, Your Honour, mark each of these with DB44B and DB45B. At some point copies will have to be made, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I see no urgency in that at least from the Trial Chamber's point of view.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Could they be taken to the ELMO, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Mr. Smailagic, I'm going to ask you to look at two documents and the usher has them in the order I'm going to ask you to look at them. We are going to put them on the ELMO so everyone can see them at the same time you do. Take your time and look at them carefully before we put on the ELMO and then I will ask you the couple of questions I have. Okay. Let's start with. Put the first document on the ELMO, please. Yes. Now this first document that's marked it says "D44B," it should say "DB44B." Mr. Smailagic, that is a, as I understand it, it's a marriage certificate; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAHUDIN SMAILAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And it shows, does it not, that Mr. Brdjanin's wife is named Mira?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAHUDIN SMAILAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And does that appear to be an authentic certificate to you?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I don't want him to answer that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I won't ask it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I want you to look now -- put on the ELMO the second document, please, which would be DB45B. And Mr. Smailagic you've had a chance to read that document?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAHUDIN SMAILAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've just read it just now.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And that document says, does it not, that Mira Brdjanin has been employed by Kameni Agregati since 1 July of 1980?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAHUDIN SMAILAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, that is, I have never heard of a company called Kameni Agregati in Banja Luka. She worked in the Kozara Agricultural company. They had several departments there. The so-called basic organisations of associated labour. As for this Kameni Agregati company, maybe it's just another name, but I'm not sure. At least I have never heard of this company, Kameni Agregati.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: So it's your position that your testimony about where she worked is correct and this document is wrong?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It doesn't necessarily follow. Ask him whether he still stands by what he stated in his previous statement. But it's not -- it doesn't necessarily follow that this document is wrong.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I'll ask that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Do you stand by what you stated a few moments ago with regard to the company that you testified that she worked for and what you saw her at? And I can't remember the name of the company.

utterances.speaker: ZIJAHUDIN SMAILAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. At the GIK Kozara, which is a construction and industrial company involved in construction business. It consisted of several departments and it originated from a merger of two or three companies in Banja Luka, Krajina company, the 1st of May company, the brick yard in Zjalozjani. Mermer, another local factory which also entered this merger so maybe that is the company in question, which eventually changed its name into this one. Several other companies that were joined and merged into this company. Some of them were originally from Banja Luka, some were from Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right. These documents can now be returned to the Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, could I ask that we be supplied with copies?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That will be taken care of. I don't need to stress the importance of it but it will be taken care of, by, I suppose, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: If the Registrar doesn't do it, I will. We will certainly have it done quickly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's your duty to do it in any case.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes, I will do it the first chance we get to get to a photocopier.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, if there is any problem if they are supplied to us over the break, we can do the photocopying ourselves.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: We have a very nice photocopier available to the Defence that sometimes works.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: So let me ask you what your position is as you sit here today. This travel agency that you talk about, is it your position that it was run by a woman named Perka or that it was run by Brdjanin's wife, whose name we now know to be Mira? Which position is it that you now take?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAHUDIN SMAILAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I say that it was run by Mrs. Perka and Radovan Glogovac.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You spoke yesterday about the ARK Crisis Staff. You don't know, do you, when that Crisis Staff was formed?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAHUDIN SMAILAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it was formed around May or June, 1992. It was in 1992. That's when it was formed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Again, can you be more specific, Mr. Ackerman, which Crisis Staff your questioning the witness about?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Whether it's the ARK one or whether it's the municipality of Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: It's the Crisis Staff of ARK that I think I'm talking about, Your Honour. I'm referring to the statement of the witness on page 4, the paragraph right under the one about Perka. Where the witness says, Mr. Smailagic, this is what your statement indicates that you said. "I am unable to say when the Crisis Staff was formed in Banja Luka. I only know that Brdjanin was the person in charge of this Crisis Staff." I assume that you are speaking there about the Crisis Staff of the Autonomous Region of Krajina; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAHUDIN SMAILAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You say, "I am unable to comment on the way the Crisis Staff operated or what level of authority it had. I only know that he was in charge of everything." Is that what you said?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAHUDIN SMAILAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was responsible for -- the Crisis Staff of the Krajina was responsible for all the organisation. Everything that happened in Banja Luka, and in Krajina, the Crisis Staff would take decisions for this. And then subordinates would implement the decisions of the Regional Crisis Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And on the previous page, you told us that the SDS was in charge of everything that happened in the area. So you've got two organisations being in charge of everything that happened in the area, correct?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAHUDIN SMAILAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that the SDS had taken power, but as a political party it had its organs, and the SDS formed the Crisis Staffs too. So that it governed the Crisis Staffs.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: It's your position that the ARK Crisis Staff was an organ of the SDS?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAHUDIN SMAILAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You don't know that it was an organ of the Assembly of the Autonomous Region of Krajina?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAHUDIN SMAILAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Assembly of the Autonomous Region of Krajina was under the control of the SDS, after all.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: It's true, is it not, that that assembly contained delegates who were not members of the SDS but were members of other parties, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAHUDIN SMAILAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. Maybe there were two other parties.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And don't you know --

utterances.speaker: ZIJAHUDIN SMAILAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know the exact number.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Don't you know that the ARK Crisis Staff was created by appointment signed by a Nikola Erceg, who was the president of the executive board of the Autonomous Region of Krajina? Do you not know that?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I am going to object to the form of that question because our case, this is -- the document is there for all to see and to use the words created by Nikola Erceg we submit is not a proper way of describing it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Ackerman, I suggest to you to rephrase your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Do you not know that the ARK Crisis Staff was created under the authority of Nikola Erceg who was the president of the executive board of ARK?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAHUDIN SMAILAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. Then in the very next sentence, after you tell us that Brdjanin was in charge of everything, you say, "I think that Brdjanin and Kupresanin were the main people in charge of things happening in the area." Correct?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAHUDIN SMAILAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That was my opinion. My opinion was that Mr. Brdjanin and Kupresanin and Stojan Zupljanin who was the chief of police, I thought they were most responsible for what was happening in Banja Luka by virtue of their function as the president of the Crisis Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, what happened to Vukic? You told us a little while ago that Vukic was president of the SDS and that they were in charge of everything. You have now taken Vukic out of power, have you?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAHUDIN SMAILAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Vukic was the president of the SDS and he was responsible to the higher organs, the higher authorities within his party and he implemented the decisions that, the orders that he received from them.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: But if you're correct that the Crisis Staff was a SDS organisation, and Brdjanin and Kupresanin were members of the SDS, then they would have been subordinate to Dr. Vukic, wouldn't they? Because he was the president.

utterances.speaker: ZIJAHUDIN SMAILAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In terms of the party, yes, they were subordinate to them.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes. There came a time, did there not, Mr. Smailagic, when you received a notice to report for a work obligation or something of that nature; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAHUDIN SMAILAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I was called up to carry out a work obligation.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And you tell us in your statement that when you received that notice, you went to complain to the Ministry of Defence and a person by the name of Djukic -- who is Djukic?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAHUDIN SMAILAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't go to complain to him, but I responded to his invitation and he was an officer -- an official in the Ministry for Defence for sending people to work obligations. As I was a disabled pensioner, I had a document, a decision, from the Disability Commission stating that I was a pensioner. When I provided him with this document, with the decision, on being unfit for any sort of physical work, he simply said that he did not admit this, that he wanted a certificate from a Serbian doctor stating that I was unfit and the deadline he set me was for the following morning. I went to the clinic and I told the doctor what the situation was. He wrote down what was necessary and I took this to the gentleman on the following day. I gave him the certificate. He simply took it and he tore it up. He didn't want to admit this, accept this, and I was in Mr. Djukic's office at the time. He was a very big man. Unfortunately I don't know his surname. He hit me several times. He was a strong man. When he hit me the first time, I fell down between the desk and the door. He maltreated me quite badly.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I think the question that I asked you was who is Djukic?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAHUDIN SMAILAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was an official for the work obligations in the Ministry. It used to be called the Military Department and then it became the Ministry, then the name changed to the Ministry of Defence. And he was employed there.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: When you told the investigator from the OTP, "When I received my notice, I went to the Ministry of Defence to complain," is it your position that you didn't use the word "complain" and that that's another area where the translation is wrong?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAHUDIN SMAILAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't even -- I didn't complain because I couldn't have complained. Until I had replied to the call-up because I thought that when I provided him with this decision I would be released. I wouldn't have to carry out the work obligation.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: What did you mean when you told the OTP investigator, "When I received my notice, I went to the Ministry of Defence to complain"? If you find that statement, please, it's on page 5 of the English version, it's at the very top of that page?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAHUDIN SMAILAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. I didn't receive an order. It was an invitation. I went to the Ministry of Defence - perhaps there is a mistake in the translation - I went to complain about responding, but one might think that I was complaining because I had the decision stating that I was unfit for any kind of physical work and I also had to respond to this notice.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I want to talk to you for a moment about the SOS barricades.

utterances.speaker: ZIJAHUDIN SMAILAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would like -- could I ask the Presiding Judge to allow me to state some more details about this call-up and to explain on what basis? If you would allow me to do so?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Smailagic, are you going to give us more information [Microphone not activated].

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, Your Honour, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Smailagic, are you saying this or are you making this request because you want to give more information than is contained already in your statement? Because I think in your statement, you gave enough information with regard to the call and with regard to what happened to you when you went to the Ministry of Defence, how you were beaten up. I don't see the relevance. If there is anything else that is so important for us to know, then I will let you say it. But if it's a repetition of what you have already stated, there is no need for it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't want to repeat anything but I would like to add something, because I didn't make any statements about how I was released from the work obligation, and I would like to clarify this matter for Mr. Ackerman and for you. But I continue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Go ahead, Mr. Smailagic. Please keep it short.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll try. After this meeting, when they tore up the statement from the doctor, I was ordered to come the following day in front of the automobile company where I would be sent for the work obligation. I didn't respond to this call-up. No one looked for me for three days. On the fourth day the military police came in the afternoon. About after 3.00, and they had an order to take me to the Ministry of Defence. I and Emir Djemesivic [phoen], a neighbour of mine, Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. and another person from the Ministry of Defence, we were welcomed, we were met by Mr. Seva and he said that he was carrying out these duties, that he was replacing Mr. Djukic who had left, who had gone on holiday. When I told him what had happened, he said, "Come to see me tomorrow and we will see about this." When I turned up, he said, "I can see that you're unfit and that you cannot work. The only thing I can suggest is go, deregister at the Ministry of Defence" and in order to do that I had to deregister with the Ministry of the Interior and to tell them I was leaving Banja Luka.
