That was in 1993. I had to tell them that I was leaving Banja Luka and it was only then that I could be released. I went there and I was then released. I told them that I was going to Slovenia, that's how I deregistered. So for a year or so, I walked around Banja Luka with a certificate of deregistration, because whoever didn't respond to this call-up was not allowed to remain in Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Mr. Ackerman, you can proceed --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: -- with your question, please. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yesterday, Mr. Smailagic, you were talking about statements that you claimed to have heard Mr. Brdjanin make and one of those statements was, I think you said, at a rally, where he said something to the effect, "You are standing on holy Serbian land," or something like that. Do you recall what I'm talking about?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAHUDIN SMAILAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Would you agree that you're mistaken and that it was Vojo Kupresanin who made that statement, in fact, made it on numerous occasions?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAHUDIN SMAILAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you see, that statement that this was holy Serbian land, most people would say that, but I remembered Mr. Brdjanin saying that because he said it on several occasions.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And what I'm asking you is wasn't it Vojo Kupresanin and not Mr. Brdjanin who said it on several occasions? You can just say yes or no.

utterances.speaker: ZIJAHUDIN SMAILAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember now. Believe me.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. I want to speak to you just very briefly about these SOS barricades that you talked about yesterday. That were set up in May of 1992. And one of the things you told us about the people in these barricades is that they were from all three ethnicities, that there were Croats, Serbs and Muslims in that organisation; correct?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAHUDIN SMAILAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And that these people manned the barricades between May of 1992 and November of 1992, when they were then taken over by regular soldiers; correct?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAHUDIN SMAILAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were there at the very start, in the month of May. I said they were well-known Banja Luka criminals, who were involved in crime before the war, too.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I think you maybe didn't understand my question. Let me repeat it. The only question I'm asking you was, the SOS people remained this these barricades until November when they were taken over by regular soldiers. I think that is your statement, is it not?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAHUDIN SMAILAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it's November, I'm not sure whether I said that or not. I'm not sure about the time. I don't know how long they were there, but I know that they were removed.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, I'm willing to accept approximately November, if that's okay with you.

utterances.speaker: ZIJAHUDIN SMAILAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I couldn't agree with that exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Okay. So can you then be precise and say when it was? If it was not around November, approximately November, when regular soldiers took over?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAHUDIN SMAILAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know when they were -- when they were placed there. And I know that they gradually left, that they were gradually removed. I know that one man was killed at the barricade. He had problems with the police. He had probably robbed someone, who wasn't a Muslim, a Serbian citizen. He stole something from him, and he was reported to police and there was a conflict and I know that one person was killed. And then they started -- they were removed. Whether it was October, September, I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Ackerman, a break is planned for ten minutes from now so that you regulate yourself.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: In your statement on page 6 you speak of a person by the name of Djordjo Babic. That is someone you know, is it not?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAHUDIN SMAILAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And Djordjo Babic is a Serb; correct?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAHUDIN SMAILAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And he lived in the same neighbourhood that you lived in, Pobrdje; correct?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAHUDIN SMAILAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And what you say in your statement, that he was dismissed from his job for being a Muslim sympathiser. Do you stand by that statement?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAHUDIN SMAILAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You say that he came to your house and told you that Muslims should not provoke Serbs. Do you stand by the statement that he came to your house?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAHUDIN SMAILAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know if he said to my house or maybe -- but I can't find it right now. I just want to remind myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: If you look at -- it's on page 6 of the English version. It's in a paragraph that starts with the language, "Weapons were being handed out to all Serbs." And further down in that paragraph, you talk about Djordjo Babic coming to your house. It's in your first statement.

utterances.speaker: ZIJAHUDIN SMAILAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First statement?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes. It's the 6th page, so that would be more than halfway through it. It would be just the last couple of pages.

utterances.speaker: ZIJAHUDIN SMAILAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Where mention is made of distributing weapons; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: That's the paragraph.

utterances.speaker: ZIJAHUDIN SMAILAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's what I was looking for. I never said that he came to my house, but he came up to my house, so that was in the street after all. My house is in a street and I have a yard and a fence. That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right. And you stand by the proposition that he said to you, "Muslims should not provoke Serbs"?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAHUDIN SMAILAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. When we spoke, he said, "You see what the situation is like? "Don't let us allow" - we called this street Mahala - "don't let them allow something happen in this street as things have happened in other places." He was very fair and he tried to help us and that's why he was replaced. But otherwise he was an official of the SDS for that part of the town

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: If you look at the next paragraph I just want to draw your attention to one sentence there, in which you say, "I only know of one incident of looting." Is that a true statement?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAHUDIN SMAILAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: One that I saw. I was able to see it through the window of my house. I also had other opportunities to see this, but I know about other cases.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: But in your statement, what you said was, "I only know of one incidents of looting." That's the language that appears there, is it not?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAHUDIN SMAILAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't say that I heard about it. I said that I saw it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You're saying that's what you said in your statement, that you saw an incident of looting?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAHUDIN SMAILAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Is that what -- is that what the translation, the B/C/S translation says? Read -- just read that paragraph, will you please n B/C/S, it starts with, "I remember soldiers searching homes," so it can be translated?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAHUDIN SMAILAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Read it out loud so that the translator can translate it into English for us, "I remember seeing soldiers." Just read that in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: ZIJAHUDIN SMAILAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "I remember that I saw soldiers, how they were searching homes in my neighbourhood. My neighbourhood -- my neighbour, Midhat Djumisic who was visited by 15 soldiers all of a sudden. I think that the soldiers thought that they would find something. And that is why so many of them came. I only know of one example of looting and that is the one that I saw, but I heard of numbers of such cases."

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Did you add to what is in the statement? Or is that language there?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAHUDIN SMAILAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what is stated there. Repeat that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Could you just read the last six words of that paragraph in that statement? The last six words?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] "I know of only one case of looting."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's it. That answers your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes, thank you, Your Honour. Let me stop here, if I may.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Ackerman. We will have a break of about 25 to 30 minutes. Resuming at noon. How much longer do you think you have Mr. Ackerman?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, it's very difficult for me to tell. I'm on page 9 of 23 pages of notes. I'm not halfway through yet.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I'm taking it that the next witness -- I hope still to get the investigator in very briefly today but I am going to take it that the next witness will not be starting today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's what I figure.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I think it will go a little faster, I hope so. It should.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. I thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Please try to bring us to a happy ending, the sooner the quicker.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Mr. Smailagic, we've made it to page 7 of your -- the English version at least of your report. And on the English version you talk about a person named Sadeta Cardzic who you talk about being found dead of strangulation. You say in that paragraph that you have no other information regarding killings in Banja Luka in the year 1991 or 1992, correct?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAHUDIN SMAILAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As regards Ms. Sadeta Cardzic the information is correct, she was found strangled in her apartment, the strangulation was performed with a so-called police wire. Nothing was missing from the apartment. It was not robbed. The body was found by her neighbour, Meliha Filipovic a few days later, they were colleagues. As for any other information regarding killings, I did have some but I was unable to confirm where or when, but there were cases of murder. However, I have no accurate information about that. As for Nermin Mesinovic, what is what his father told me so that is one case that I know for sure, and I know of other cases of people having been beaten up, for example, but I didn't want to mention any other case of murder because I was not sure. I did not have any reliable information of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Did you hear any bombs going off in Banja Luka in 1992, at night?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAHUDIN SMAILAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. There were several such incidents. As for shooting, that was a daily occurrence.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I didn't ask you about shooting. I asked you if you heard any bombs going off at night and you say you did, yes?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAHUDIN SMAILAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Explosions, hand grenades going off.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: How many nights during 1992 would you say you heard bombs going off?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAHUDIN SMAILAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Several times. I couldn't tell you whether it was five, ten or 15 times. We didn't count them. We almost got used to them at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: 15 nights would be an outside number, in terms of the most you'd have heard? Would you even say maybe 20 nights?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAHUDIN SMAILAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you mean one after the other, in sequence, no. When I say that there were explosions I am referring to a probably greater number than the one you stated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment, Mr. Ackerman. This period of time, where were you actually living in Banja Luka? What was your place of residence?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I lived in my house in Hadzihalilovic [phoen] Street.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: In Banja Luka or in --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Pobrdje is in Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's why I wanted to know exactly which part of -- the suburb of Banja Luka, no?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Not exactly a suburb. It is relatively close to the centre of the town, as I said, I am perhaps five minutes walk away from Hotel Palace, for example.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: What I'd like you to do and I don't need you to be accurate about this, I only want your best estimate and just the best you can do, I don't expect you to be accurate, I don't expect you to have made a list or anything like that. How many nights during the year 1992, would you say that you heard bombs going off?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAHUDIN SMAILAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't want to exaggerate so I shall say between 15 and 20, if not more than that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. There were mosques and churches that were destroyed in Banja Luka. Those destructions all happened in the year 1993, didn't they?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAHUDIN SMAILAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The mosques, yes, but not all of the churches. There were orthodox churches and Catholic churches. As far as I know, one of them -- one such church was in Petricovac. That church, I know, was destroyed. As for the other two, they were not destroyed, these two Catholic churches, that I know of.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: The only question is, you say in your statement that the -- there was one Catholic church in Banja Luka destroyed in 1993. That's the one you're referring to, is it not?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAHUDIN SMAILAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And my question really is that it happened in 1993.

utterances.speaker: ZIJAHUDIN SMAILAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I couldn't confirm that, whether it was in 1993 precisely.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, you think you had it right in your statement to the OTP back in 2001, when you told them that it was in 1993?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAHUDIN SMAILAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Most probably that was the case. However, in view of the fact that many things were going on at the time in Banja Luka, it is easy to get confused. But I am almost certain about that, because the mosques were being destroyed throughout 1993, so it is possible that this church was also destroyed in 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: When you gave this statement to the Prosecutor in April of 2000, you were making an effort to tell the truth, were you not?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAHUDIN SMAILAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. To the best of my recollection.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: ZIJAHUDIN SMAILAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course, with the possibility of getting mixed up in respect of dates, even years. But I was not confused about the event itself. I'm sure that that was indeed done.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm skipping a bunch of material here. That's why it's taking me a moment to get organised.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I want you to look, Mr. Smailagic, at page 3 of your second statement. This is the one where you were correcting some things from your first statement. And on page 3, you indicate that there were two Crisis Staffs operating in Banja Luka, a municipal staff and an ARK Crisis Staff; correct?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAHUDIN SMAILAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: With regard to the municipal Crisis Staff, you indicate that the members of the municipal Crisis Staff included Brdjanin, Vukic, Radic, Zupljanin, Kupresanin, Cavic, Kasagic and others; correct?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAHUDIN SMAILAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that the municipal Crisis Staff was headed by --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I haven't got the LiveNote here. Those were the people he identified part as the ARK Crisis Staff and part as the municipal. I don't recall him saying that Brdjanin, Vukic and Zupljanin were members of the municipal. But I may be wrong. I don't have the note.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think, Ms. Korner, I think Mr. Ackerman is reading, referring specifically to a three line paragraph there is in the middle of the page.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I see. I'm sorry, I thought he was referring to the evidence he gave yesterday. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Second statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Page 3 of the second statement, actually it's the second page of the statement but it reads, "I think that the entire SDS executive board were members of the municipal Crisis Staff, including Brdjanin, Vukic, Predrag Radic, Stojan Zupljanin, Vojo Kupresanin, Cavic, Rajko Kasagic and others." So the question, if you please, repeat it, Mr. Ackerman?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You say in your statement there, do you not, Mr. Smailagic, that Brdjanin was a member of the municipal Crisis Staff? Correct?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAHUDIN SMAILAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said he was the president of the Regional Crisis Staff. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Would you please look at a paragraph that the Judge just read beginning with the words, "I think that the entire SDS executive board were members of the municipal Crisis Staff." Do you find that paragraph?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAHUDIN SMAILAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: In that paragraph, you name Mr. Brdjanin as a member of the municipal Crisis Staff, don't you?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAHUDIN SMAILAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes, that's what is stated here, but when I was giving my statement, I was referring to the composition of both Crisis Staffs, and I offered the names that are stated here. Some of them were members of the municipal, and the others members of the regional staff. There may have been a mistake, either in recording or in translation. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, does your signature appear at the bottom of that page? Well, actually it would be in the English version. It was read to you before you signed it, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAHUDIN SMAILAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And then after it was read to you, and you were satisfied that it was correct, you signed it; right?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAHUDIN SMAILAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Is it your position that somebody has changed this document since you signed it and put Brdjanin in there as a member of the municipal Crisis Staff when you didn't say that?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAHUDIN SMAILAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think that anybody has changed the document. Maybe I was misunderstood. You must understand the situation I was in at the time, and the situation I'm in today. It's possible that I confused something, but as far as I am concerned, it was not important whether they were members of the regional or the municipal staff. What was important was the fact that they were involved in the decision-making process, both in the municipal and the regional staff. In the municipal Crisis Staff carried out the orders, instructions of the Regional Crisis Staff. Whether someone was a member of the regional or a municipal staff, as far as I am concerned, was one -- amounted to one and the same thing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. If my memory doesn't fail me, Mr. Ackerman, you put the same question yesterday and you had the same answer yesterday. Or if it wasn't you, it was someone else, but definitely, the witness has already stated before what he's just reiterated now.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I think your memory is of a similar question I put to Mr. -- the other witness, the previous witness, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No, no. This witness. In other words, that he told you that for all intents and purposes, it was an interchanging persons. Any way, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I'm finished with the issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I do want to ask you, Mr. Smailagic, if you are taking seriously this procedure and trying to give us true answers when I ask you questions or if you feel under some kind of pressure and you're just kind of guessing at things.

utterances.speaker: ZIJAHUDIN SMAILAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Quite the contrary. I'm actually very glad that you're asking me these questions. I'm really doing my best, and I'm trying to provide you with my sincere answers. However, I appeal to your understanding of what I have been through. It is quite easy to mix things up. I would need considerable amount of time to set everything right. I don't think I have this opportunity at the moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: That's fine. Thank you. I understand what you've been through and that that was a difficult period in your life. I want to go to the very end of your second statement now. You talked yesterday about being indicted for espionage. You say in your statement, it's a paragraph that begins with, "The investigating judge Stevo Stupar interrogated me prior to the trial." You say, "He accused me of several charges and I agreed to all of them because I had no choice. The guards were standing next to me and I felt very intimidated." Correct?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAHUDIN SMAILAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: At the actual trial of the case, then, after that appearance, did you feel intimidated in the same way at your actual trial?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAHUDIN SMAILAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you're referring to the courtroom itself, I felt protected. I knew that nothing could happen to me there. However, there were preparations made before that. I was -- that is, before we were taken to the investigating judge, we would be beaten up in the cell before that and we would be warned as to what we would say. They would tell us, "Be careful what you say to the judge."

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: In your actual trial, though you felt tree free to actually state your Defence that you really didn't know what was in the various factions that you were sending to various places? That was basically your defence, wasn't it, that you didn't know the contents, either they were in code or you had not read them?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAHUDIN SMAILAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Okay. We will get to that in a minute. I want to ask you about -- you talked on direct about the lawyers that were assigned to you and the first lawyer, a gentleman named Opacic had actually asked your wife for money and when your wife couldn't pay him, he abandoned you; correct?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAHUDIN SMAILAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And then you told us about Ms. Maglov being assigned. She didn't ask your wife for any money, did she?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAHUDIN SMAILAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. She never met my wife, nor did she ever meet me.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You know a lawyer named Meliha Filipovic?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAHUDIN SMAILAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: She was also involved in this case, was she not?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAHUDIN SMAILAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, she was. She was representing her brother.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Safet Filipovic?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAHUDIN SMAILAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And she is a Muslim lawyer; correct?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAHUDIN SMAILAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And she proceeded in the case in the same manner as Ms. Maglov did, didn't she?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAHUDIN SMAILAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. She acted opposite.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Opposite in what way?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAHUDIN SMAILAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Compared to Ms. Maglov, who was supposed to defend me. She did her best to defend her brother, her client, that is.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: She made arguments in court, she questioned witnesses, she did the kind of things that I'm doing here today? Is that your testimony?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAHUDIN SMAILAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Isn't it correct that at the time of this trial, that all of you who were charged in the case, were aware that you were going to be exchanged?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAHUDIN SMAILAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, we were not.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Excuse me just a second.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I want the witness to be shown one of the exhibits, it's DB0043B.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Mr. Smailagic, you now have the Exhibit DB0043B. Do you recognise that document?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAHUDIN SMAILAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This is a statement that I gave to the Security Services Centre in Banja Luka in 1994.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And you were asked about that document by the investigator from the OTP in your second statement, and I think you told the investigator from OTP that it is only a partly accurate reflection of what you told the investigators in 1994 when the statement was taken. Is that a fair statement?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAHUDIN SMAILAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right. I want to refer you to what is on page 2 of the statement. It's right at the very -- I don't know if it's at the very top of the page in B/C/S but it refers to the two Merhamet organisations the MDD and the MHD. Do you find that reference?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAHUDIN SMAILAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Is that in the first one or in the second one?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: It's in the one I just handed you, the Exhibit which is DB0043B. It was just handed you by the usher?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAHUDIN SMAILAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's here.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I misdirected. You. It's just right on the top of the second page. There should be some discussion about the two Merhamets, MDD and MHD?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: In B/C/S it's on page 3, the very last paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour, you're right. That's where it is. As usual.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You've read it. Is -- could you tell us about this effort to merge the two Merhamets, and why they were not merged in the first place?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAHUDIN SMAILAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were certain internal conflicts in the Merhamet with regard to the organisation of the kitchen. Some were against it. And this is where the first rift appeared.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: The first rift between who?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAHUDIN SMAILAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Between the leaders, in the Merhamet itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Part of the problem, was it not, that one of the Merhamets was registered in Banja Luka, Republika Srpska, and there were people that objected to that?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAHUDIN SMAILAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: This fellow, Nijaz Karaselimovic you say was a person whom they called a Chetnik. Who called him a Chetnik?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAHUDIN SMAILAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you see, I had to -- I was forced to write quite a few of these sentences in this statement. They were dictated to me. I just had to sign it. I have to go back a little. To the first interview in the Security Services Centre. My attention was immediately drawn to the fact that I had to answer the questions and to confirm what they told me. I didn't even read this statement. I had to sign it in the Security Services Centre --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Mr. Smailagic --

utterances.speaker: ZIJAHUDIN SMAILAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was about 2.00 a.m.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: The reason I asked you at the beginning --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let him finish, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I'm sorry. He's talking about a completely different statement, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: He's talking about a statement to the Security Services Centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Not this one. He's talking about a his first statement to the security services.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Which statement are you referring to as you give evidence now, Mr. Smailagic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The one which I made in the Security Services Centre, the one that the gentleman asked me about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The one that you have in front of you now?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, the one that I just received.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So you were telling us, Mr. Smailagic, that this was not even read out to you, that you were made to sign, that some sentences were even inserted there without you -- without reflecting what you had stated or without you saying those words? What else do you want to tell us, in reply to Mr. Ackerman's question?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In this text which is before me, many things were added, many things that I didn't say. The fact that they called Mr. Karaselimovic a Chetnik, I heard this in the security services centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: The reason I asked you at the beginning about what you said to the OTP regarding this statement being only a partly accurate reflection of what you said was to be fair to you, and to give you the opportunity, when I ask you about things in the statement, to say that this was something you did not say. And I understand that it's your position that there are things in this statement that you did not say. And what I'm asking you is, if you said these things, and if so, what was meant by them. I have, I think, one more thing to ask you about with regard to the statement and, that is the very next sentence, which says, "Jakirlic claimed that Krzic, intentionally --" well it's actually two sentences. "At this same time, Jakirlic attacked Krzic over an interview that he had given to the media. Jakirlic claimed that Krzic intentionally put all of Banja Luka's Muslims in great jeopardy so that he could get away." Did you say that? Is that part of your statement?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAHUDIN SMAILAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, they were talking about this after Krzic had left Banja Luka, and Krzic's statement was related to talk about a NATO intervention. And when NATO planes started controlling the air space above Banja Luka, and when the planes appeared, he said that he was happy and so on. Jakirlic reacted to this and said for -- "For the sake of our security, he shouldn't have stated something like this."

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: If you look near the bottom, I don't know if it's near the bottom of the page or not, let me see if I can find it for you. It's about one, two, three, it's about the fourth paragraph after the one we've been looking at. It may even be the final paragraph of the document. Let me see. No. It's -- it's a paragraph that says, "I heard that the money earmarked for the Banja Luka Merhamet which Krzic had embezzled was later transferred to Sarajevo." Did you in fact make a statement that Mr. Krzic had embezzled some money? Or was that one of the things that was added to your statement?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAHUDIN SMAILAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't say that, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: ZIJAHUDIN SMAILAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't even remember this question being put to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right. That's fine. There was a question put to you about the organisation Valter and what the statement says your answer was that it was a secret organisation established by Muharem Krzic. Is that true or is it not true?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAHUDIN SMAILAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's true that that is what it says in the statement. "I was forced to do this in the security services centre, because one of the documents, one document was found and it was signed 'Valter.'"

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Could I ask now that the witness be provided with the document P465? I don't know if that was divided properly into P465 A and B. If it was the one I'm looking for is the B version?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: This is the judgement, no?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes, it is, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Of the military court Banja Luka, 1st September, 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I want you to find the B/C/S version and I want to direct you to page 2. Right at the top of page 2, you will see the number 3, followed by your name. Have you found that?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAHUDIN SMAILAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I want to ask you if it's correct in that paragraph where it speaks of you having been convicted of an offence in September of 1962 and sentenced to eight months in prison.

utterances.speaker: ZIJAHUDIN SMAILAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And could you tell us what offence that was you were convicted of?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAHUDIN SMAILAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't speak about that now.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: It's correct, is it not, that you were convicted of embezzlement?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAHUDIN SMAILAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's how it was formulated, but that wasn't the matter. That's how it was formulated. Some damage was done.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: This was not a -- this was way before the war. This was a regular court. And you were convicted and sentenced to eight months. Did you actually serve prison time?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAHUDIN SMAILAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: The document also indicates that you were later convicted of another offence and sentenced to three months' imprisonment?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAHUDIN SMAILAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: What was that for?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAHUDIN SMAILAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was related to the work organisation, but ...

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: These offences both involved offences of dishonesty, did they not?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAHUDIN SMAILAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to this, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: In the beginning of your testimony here, you talked about these meetings that were held in 1961 that you claim that Mr. Brdjanin was part of. These meetings mainly dealt with issues of mobilisation, did they not?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAHUDIN SMAILAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not just mobilisation but other conditions in the town of Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: One of the problems that was going -- perceived as a problem that was going on at that time was that there was a war going on in Croatia and Muslims were resisting mobilisation and resisting fighting in that war because Izetbegovic had told them it was not their war and they shouldn't go fight in it; correct?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAHUDIN SMAILAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not that it wasn't their war but that it wasn't a war that they should engage in.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And this war was going on before the independence of Bosnia-Herzegovina was declared or accepted; correct?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAHUDIN SMAILAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And there were also Serbs who were refusing to be mobilised? In fact, they were leaving Banja Luka to try to hide from being mobilised, were they not?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAHUDIN SMAILAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There was several such cases.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And any sanctions that were promised against people who refused to be mobilised applied equally to Serbs and Muslims, isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAHUDIN SMAILAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You spoke about these rallies that you attended in 1992. You said there may have been as many as seven of them, and you talked about provocative things that were said by the various speakers at these Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. rallies. These were rallies of the SDS, I think you told us; correct?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAHUDIN SMAILAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And it would have been -

utterances.speaker: ZIJAHUDIN SMAILAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: It would have been mostly Serbs that were attending those rallies; correct?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAHUDIN SMAILAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mostly Serbs, but there were other people too, many people went there out of curiosity, and one always expected to find out additional information.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: How many fights or riots or things of that nature broke out during these rallies or immediately thereafter?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAHUDIN SMAILAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were no revolts, as far as I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Were you ever assaulted by anyone for being at these rallies?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAHUDIN SMAILAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You told us about seeing Mr. Brdjanin on TV in 1992. Wasn't that difficult because of the lack of electricity? How could you watch TV with no electricity?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAHUDIN SMAILAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There is a very simple explanation. In the street in which I lived, there was electricity on one side of the street on one day and on the next day the other side of the street had electricity so as neighbours we would visit each other and watch television.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Weren't there large periods of time when neither side of the street had no electricity, when the whole city of Banja Luka was basically cut off from electricity?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAHUDIN SMAILAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was later on in 1993, I think, but it was never the case that the entire city of Banja Luka was without electricity. At least as far as I can remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: After the war started, didn't the Bosnian government shut off the electrical supply from Tuzla so that Banja Luka did not have electricity, as part of the war effort?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAHUDIN SMAILAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I know that they had electricity. But in the -- later on, around 1993, that was when electricity often disappeared, the whole street lacked electricity. We then used generators and we were able to watch television.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Many of the people who were employed in Banja Luka worked at various factories and plants there, did they not?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAHUDIN SMAILAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And when you talk about people not being able to work, not being employed, that arose to a great deal, a great extent, from the fact that factories and plants can't operate without electricity, so there was no reason for people to go to work. They couldn't work. And it was both Serbs and Muslims who were unable to go to work because of the lack of electricity to run the plants and the factories; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAHUDIN SMAILAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, the factories, the tobacco factory had electricity. The shoe factory had electricity. The regular hospital. All the important institutions and large companies had electricity. Rudi Cajavac also had electricity. Kosmos, especially the two ones that were involved in military production, Vrbas and Kosmos.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You told us that at one of these rallies you attended, Mr. Brdjanin said, "Whoever is not with us is against us."

utterances.speaker: ZIJAHUDIN SMAILAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You actually heard that?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAHUDIN SMAILAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Did you hear George Bush say that?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAHUDIN SMAILAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: George Bush?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: ZIJAHUDIN SMAILAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. After this -- after what happened when he said that whoever isn't with us is against us. Something to that effect, yes, I heard that on television. When he was referring to this coalition.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Someone more important said it also about 2.000 years ago, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: More important than George Bush, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Oh, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You talked about the restriction of movements in Banja Luka, and that persons without passes would be arrested if they tried to move around the town of Banja Luka, correct?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAHUDIN SMAILAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And they were taken away to do work obligations. They were usually taken to do very hard work, digging trenches at the front lines, but even people who had passes and who had work obligations when they would come to Banja Luka and when they would go out, they would sometimes show their passes and the passes would be torn up.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: This had to do, did it not, with the mobilisation issue, that people were being found who had not responded to mobilisation and then forced into some kind of public service, and that that included both Muslims and Serbs and Croats?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAHUDIN SMAILAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know how the work obligation was organised, but as far as I'm concerned, I know how this worked. I know that all Muslims and at the time the -- all Croats too, had an obligation, and they had to respond to this summons to carry out work obligations.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And you know that Serbs who were called up were sent off to the front to fight in the war?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAHUDIN SMAILAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Serbs who received this summons for work obligations, they remained in the town, they took up the positions, these work positions, for which there were an insufficient -- there was an insufficient number of people. As far as the Muslims are concerned, I know for sure that at the beginning, it was provocative, they first started trying to get Banja Luka intellectuals to work. They would send them to a little river and to clear the bottom of the river and this was often very humiliating.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You knew that Serbs were being mobilised into the army and being sent to Croatia to fight in the war in Croatia, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAHUDIN SMAILAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they went there.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And you knew that Muslims and Croats did not want to go fight in the war in Croatia for whatever reason, and that a substitute for that was a work obligation that did not require them to go fight in the war, Croats against Croats, or Muslims against Croats. That's true, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAHUDIN SMAILAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Could you drive your car? Do you have a car? Did you have a car at that time?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAHUDIN SMAILAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Could people drive their cars freely around Banja Luka at that time, go wherever they wanted to?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAHUDIN SMAILAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: People could drive their cars around freely, if anyone had a car. But at the time, they were -- the Muslims had started selling their cars.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: What would happen if you were driving your car around Banja Luka and you went to one of these checkpoints?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAHUDIN SMAILAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They would probably seize the car and this happened. In quite a few cases they mobilised the car. They seized the car.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Talking about these SOS checkpoints again, I think you told us that you really never had any dealings with the SOS checkpoints because they weren't set up in Pobrdje, the village that you lived in; correct?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAHUDIN SMAILAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's not the village of Pobrdje. I have to make a correction. As I explained a little earlier on, it's quite close to the centre. You could consider it to be the centre of the town. There were no barricades or obstacles in that part.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And that's a heavily Muslim area, is it not?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAHUDIN SMAILAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And it's true that you didn't really have any encounters with the SOS people that were manning the barricades, did you?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAHUDIN SMAILAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No direct encounters, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: How is it that you are able to tell the Chamber that these were all well-known Banja Luka criminals, if you didn't even see them?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAHUDIN SMAILAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't say that I never saw them. I saw them. Let's say from the centre of the town, if you head towards the Rebrovac neighbourhood or towards Mejdan, on that side of the bridge, there is a barricade, on that side of Vrbas, and you could easily approach that place and see them on the other side of the river. They would walk around the town. I would come across them. They had caps on their heads with the letters SOS on the caps. And they were very arrogant. They would shoot in the centre of the town, and no one would do anything to them. They shooted in an uncontrolled manner.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: How would you know who was a well-known criminal in Banja Luka? I mean, were there photos put up around town of well-known criminals? Or how would you know that?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAHUDIN SMAILAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, let me tell you, I was born in Banja Luka. I knew almost everyone in Banja Luka. These people were people who had grown up in Banja Luka, the people that I knew personally.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And the police just let well-known criminals wander around Banja Luka at will? They didn't arrest them?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAHUDIN SMAILAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were arrested before the war. However, during this war, nobody touched them, nobody bothered them. That's exactly what they were used for.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: So are you saying these are people who before the war had been charged with crimes, had been arrested, had been charged, perhaps had been in prison and now were part of this SOS group? Is that what you're telling us?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAHUDIN SMAILAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I'd like the witness to be provided with Exhibit P254, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You looked at this exhibit yesterday, I think, Mr. Smailagic; correct?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAHUDIN SMAILAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, not until yesterday. I saw it when it was published in the newspaper. That's what I said.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes. And one of the things you told us yesterday about the faxes you were sending and the work your group was doing, was that you were doing it because you were loyal to the government of Bosnia-Herzegovina and felt in connection with that loyalty, that you needed to provide this information to various people. That's true, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAHUDIN SMAILAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: This document that you're looking at is dated 22 June, 1992; right?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAHUDIN SMAILAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: The war was going on then; correct?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAHUDIN SMAILAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the war had already started.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: The Serbs were fighting basically against the Muslims and Croats and sometimes against -- with the Croats against the Muslims and sometimes with -- against Muslims and Croats. But in any event there was a war going on involving Serbs and Muslims, correct?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAHUDIN SMAILAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And one of the things that happens in a war is that the parties in a war will try to protect their various assets, the information, their public property, their plants and facilities important for the economy, from infiltration and sabotage by the other side during a war. That's what happens in wars, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAHUDIN SMAILAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, more or less. It is just that, if I may add, we never considered this war to be a war of Serbs against Muslims but a specific group of people, of terrorists, who terrorised both Muslims and Croats alike in 1993 and who endeavoured to undermine the officially recognised state of Bosnia and Herzegovina. That is to divide it up.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, this group of terrorists, as you call them, were the SDS, which comprised most of the Serb population of Bosnia-Herzegovina, who declared an independent state, just like Bosnia-Herzegovina did, of Republika Srpska, and were in the process of trying to protect the independence that they had declared with the will of all of their people. Now you can call them terrorists, if you want, but that's exactly what happened, is it?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No. Exactly what happened, Your Honour, is a matter for you, the Judges, to decide. Mr. Ackerman can put this in the form of a question but cannot assert as a fact that the SDS and the Serbs who voted in the referendum were exerting the will of their people and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Ackerman, I think Ms. Korner's objection is correct and I would invite to you rephrase your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour, I guess I don't understand the objection. I think I asked a leading question that he could either affirm or deny and I think I'm permitted to ask a leading question on cross but I'll try to ask it in a different way.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: If it's not clear, the objection is that to assert as a fact the SDS which comprised most of the Serb population, I don't know whether there is any evidence of that, of Bosnia-Herzegovina, who declared an independent state and so on and so forth, and were in the process of trying to protect the independence they had declared with the will of their people. Your Honour, this case is exactly concerned with whether that is a correct assertion, an incorrect assertion.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: That's absolutely right. And this is a witness who has knowledge with regard to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I should be able to ask him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But actually, you wrote there -- it's as if you have written your version of the history of the events that formed the background of this case. I mean, just put the question, rephrase it, divide it and subdivide it, and if it's the case of the witness answering those questions, he will be allowed to answer those questions. If it's the case of an opinion that being -- that is being sought from the witness, which the Chamber thinks the witness is not the best qualified or is not even qualified at all to answer, then he will not be allowed to answer the question. That's the position. That's why I think Ms. Korner's objection is --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour. I should have objected earlier because this whole line of questioning is going to lead to this sort of answer. This witness thinks they are terrorists. Mr. Ackerman's case for his client is that they are not, that they are protecting, but neither is in the position to deal with this. The whole line of questioning is it started with, "Isn't it right that people in war are allowed to do that?" This is asking for opinion and he got the opinion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But you did not object then.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I know and I wish I had.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: There were some questions which -- I mean, would have taken for granted that Mr. Smailagic was sitting in my place rather than where he is sitting now. Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I just want for the record to say that I think I asked a proper, leading question and that I should be permitted to ask it. I will do as the Court directs and try to rephrase it in a way that's acceptable.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Ackerman

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Mr. Smailagic, the question I want to ask you is this: There was a declaration of independence of what came to be called Republika Srpska in 1992, isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAHUDIN SMAILAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but it was an illegal declaration and it was not recognised by the world.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Smailagic, please don't add more trouble to what we have already. Are you a lawyer by profession? Are you a constitutional lawyer? Are you deciding the case? So please refrain from making such statements that it was an illegal declaration of independence or whether it was an illegal decision and political act. Just answer the question, yes or no.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And that entity called Republika Srpska was involved in a war with an entity called Bosnia-Herzegovina in 1992; correct?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAHUDIN SMAILAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was not an entity at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: It was recognised -- well, I don't want to get into this. I'm not going to go to that. The question that I want to ask you is this: Isn't it true that just as this document removes people who are not loyal to Republika Srpska from important positions, like access to information, protection of public property, positions of importance for the functioning of the economy, just as this document does that, the government of Bosnia-Herzegovina was removing Serbs from the same kinds of positions in Bosnia-Herzegovina, doing exactly the same thing. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I thought we'd already dealt with whatever other governments may have been doing, the question is what was this particular organisation in Banja Luka doing? And as I understand, Your Honour said earlier on we were not concerned with whether or not the Muslims or the Croats had done things as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Ackerman, what do you have to state?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I think we must be very concerned with that. This is just the kind of thing governments do when they are in war. This is being portrayed to you, Your Honour, as some kind of ethnic cleansing conspiracy, and it's just what governments do when a war is going on. My government does it. Your government does it. Any government I know that's ever been at war removes people from sensitive positions that could be a threat to the war effort. It happens all the time. And this is not some grand conspiracy and that's all I'm trying to show is that the Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Muslims did the same thing with Serbs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Are you aware, Mr. Smailagic, Mr. Ackerman asked you -- asked you whether you were aware that the government of Bosnia-Herzegovina was, on its part, also removing Serbs from the same kinds of position in Bosnia-Herzegovina, doing in other words, exactly the same thing that Republika Srpska was doing. Are you aware of this event? Are you aware that this was being done by the government of Bosnia-Herzegovina? Just answer yes or no.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I cannot give you a simple answer. I know that they didn't, and as a proof, I know that Mr. Mirko Pejanovic and Tatiana Lujic [phoen] were members of the presidency and they were both of Serb ethnicity. And as for Sarajevo, and this is something that I learned recently in Zenica, Tuzla and Travnik, wherever there were appropriate conditions Serbs were working along side Muslims and there was no difference whatsoever.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So your answer is no. Yes, Mr. Ackerman?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I want to ask you about the red Kombi that you talked about. Did you ever see it?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAHUDIN SMAILAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Okay. Do you know how much territory was covered by what was called the Autonomous Region of Krajina?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAHUDIN SMAILAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Approximately, I cannot tell you how many kilometres the territory was wide but it included quite a number -- quite a few municipalities, Prijedor, Kotor Varos, Sanski Most, as regards the western part of the country.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Do you have any idea how many municipalities were actually members of the Autonomous Region of Krajina?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAHUDIN SMAILAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would have to enumerate them.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I don't need you to do that. There were several; correct?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAHUDIN SMAILAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: When you were giving your testimony yesterday, you were asked by Dr. Richterova about the members of the ARK Crisis Staff, and your answer, as I recall it, was Brdjanin, Kupresanin, Zupljanin and persons from neighbouring towns. Do you remember the names of any of the persons from neighbouring towns who were members of the Crisis Staff, ARK Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAHUDIN SMAILAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot remember, believe me, I just cannot.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Do you remember the neighbouring towns that people on the ARK Crisis Staff were from?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAHUDIN SMAILAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My main interest, of course, was Banja Luka. Whether the person was from Prijedor, for example, that's quite possible, or from Sanski Most, Drvar, I couldn't tell you their names, though. But all municipalities were represented.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes. I thank you very much. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, the position is as follows: We resumed the sitting at 12.00. Usually we stop after an hour and a half. I would like to know from the interpreters whether we could, rather than stopping at 1.30, which would be an hour and a half, whether we could go right through a quarter to 2.00, which is the time when we usually finish; that's number 1. And secondly, from Maitre de Roux, how long he anticipates his cross-examination of the witness to last. MR. DE ROUX: [Interpretation] Mr. President, in view of the cross-examination of Mr. Ackerman, I can say that my cross-examination will be significantly shorter. I will deal with certain specific issues that were not covered. I cannot promise you that I will finish in a half an hour, but I will cover a certain number of issues within that half hour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And the interpreters, please can we go on until quarter to 2.00? Okay. Thank you. So Mr. Smailagic, you are now going to be cross-examined by Maitre de Roux, the lead counsel for General Talic. Thank you. Maitre de Roux, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. DE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Smailagic, you testified that the SDA, of which you were a member, was in favour of a preservation of Yugoslavia, that is, of a federal state initially. My question is as follows: Why, therefore, while you were preparing the referendum for independence, you identified -- that is, you attempted to identify Muslim voters of the Banja Luka region?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAHUDIN SMAILAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was not our intent to establish that. This is something that happened when we received the lists from the state government. We couldn't organise the referendum without receiving this from the electoral commission. And as we couldn't obtain the paper in Banja Luka, we requested the same paper from Sarajevo, and that is how we ended up with this list of names, and in particular, the list of Muslim voters. As for the referendum itself and what you mentioned initially, though I should like you to repeat your question, that is the part that concerned the SDA and Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. DE
utterances.text: By all means. Speaking of the referendum that was under way, we referred to two specific figures, and the way that some of the citizens declared themselves as Muslims in 1991, and also another figure which you established, that is the figure of 52.000 Muslims or Bosniaks in 1992. What was the reason of this work that was done to -- in that respect? What was the objective of that work?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAHUDIN SMAILAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Various steps of manipulation started at that time involving these figures, 28.000, 52.000. It was because of that that we wanted to establish the exact number of Muslims living in Banja Luka. If I tell you that Banja Luka, the Banja Luka town, was a predominantly Muslim town, that is true. I am certain about that. As for what you stated about the SDA and its politics in favour of Yugoslavia, I addressed the issue in my statement yesterday. Yugoslavia was the best possible option for Muslims initially. However, after the secession of Croatia and Slovenia, that country no longer existed so we had to focus ourselves and orient ourselves towards Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. DE
utterances.text: I understand that position. However, there is a problem there. Other witnesses have addressed the issue of second-class citizens because they had refused mobilisation. The mobilisation concerned the front line in Croatia. However, at that time, Bosnia still was part of this federal state. So why did Bosniaks prefer to take this position in favour of Croats than in favour of Yugoslavia? Why was it a better option for them?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAHUDIN SMAILAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, Bosniaks did not commit themselves in any way. They did not side with Croats. In the meantime, Croatia had already been proclaimed as a republic, and there was nothing left for us. I mean, we didn't see any other option, as far as we were concerned in Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. DE
utterances.text: Precisely. The three constituent peoples were represented in Bosnia and Herzegovina. Didn't you think it dangerous that at the time when the federation was disintegrating because of nationalism, rampant nationalism, were you not afraid that the same thing might occur in Bosnia, that the same thing might happen to Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAHUDIN SMAILAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Frankly speaking, maybe we were naive. At the beginning of the war in Croatia, we didn't believe that the same thing could happen in Bosnia and Herzegovina. At the time we trusted the former Yugoslav People's Army because of its rhetorics and its origins, the way it was established. We believed that the army would prevent the worst from happening in Bosnia. Unfortunately, that's not what eventually happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. DE
utterances.text: However, in 1992, that is during the relevant times, the time period indicated in the indictment, the year of 1992, I think that yesterday you agreed with what Mr. Gutman, the journalist said, when he spoke about 50.000 Muslims and Croats living in Banja Luka in September, 1992. My question in relation to that would be as follows: According to you, when did this exodus of Muslims begin?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAHUDIN SMAILAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As early as late April, early May, 1992. The first mass departure occurred in mid-May. It was an organised departure. I don't know who participated in the organisation thereof. I cannot say anything about that. All I know was that military vehicles and transporters arrived and whoever wanted to leave Banja Luka was given opportunity to do so. Trouble started in Banja Luka as early as 1991, it was caused mainly by the members of the army. It consisted of various forms of intimidation. There were several departures from Banja Luka on buses. They were not prevented from leaving the town. So that was probably the reason for the significant decrease in the number of population, because a lot of citizens had already left the town.

utterances.speaker: MR. DE
utterances.text: I'm interested in the dates, because we agreed, actually you, you yourself, mentioned the number of 52.000 Muslims in Banja Luka, as opposed to the official number which was, I think, 24.000. That number concerned the year of 1991. However, you expressed your agreement with the statement made by Mr. Gutman, who spoke about 50.000 Muslims and Croats living in Banja Luka in September, 1992, which means that by the month of September, 1992, very few citizens had left. So let me ask my question once again: When do you think the exodus actually commenced?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAHUDIN SMAILAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It commenced in 1992, and continued for a while. People left the town in waves.

utterances.speaker: MR. DE
utterances.text: Very well. Do you think that the arrival of Serbs who had been expelled from Croatia could have affected the situation in Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAHUDIN SMAILAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It affected it considerably. It caused unrest. It instilled unrest amongst the population of Banja Luka, both the Croatian and Bosniak community.

utterances.speaker: MR. DE
utterances.text: How many Serbs in your opinion found refuge in Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAHUDIN SMAILAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know the exact figure. But I know that a large number of them came. They started arriving from Slavonia in 1991. I remember discussing the issue with some friends of mine, when the first group, such group, arrived. They were accommodated in a gym near the place where I live, and we took pity on them. We went to buy some food and we took that to them. We wanted to alleviate the situation for them as much as we could.

utterances.speaker: MR. DE
utterances.text: Prior to the proclamation of independence of Croatia, there had been certain events in Croatia involving the federal army, which was ethnically mixed. This army was at one point in time encircled in their barracks and they suffered considerable losses in Croatia. Don't you think that the refusal of mobilisation was a sign of defiance vis-a-vis the federal army?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAHUDIN SMAILAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think that, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. DE
utterances.text: You played an active role in local Banja Luka politics. You testified about informing the relevant authorities in Sarajevo, your ambassador through the United Nations and the representatives of the international community, of the way you perceived the situation as it was on a daily basis. Do you really think that it was a merely political role that you played at the time, the fact that you forwarded this type of information?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAHUDIN SMAILAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. My role was not only political. It was also a humanitarian role. In particular, I am referring to the international humanitarian organisations to that effect.

utterances.speaker: MR. DE
utterances.text: However, the messages that you endeavoured to transmit, according to the transcript, were coded messages. They were done according to a system which was developed by Mr. Krzic. Did it not seem strange to you that it was necessary to transmit this type of information through coded messages?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAHUDIN SMAILAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In view of the times, nothing seemed strange to me. The gentleman in question was my superior, so to speak, and I didn't feel any need to inquire further what it was all about. I thought that it was perfectly normal.

utterances.speaker: MR. DE
utterances.text: When you say that Mr. Krzic was your superior, what does this mean exactly?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAHUDIN SMAILAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was the president of the Party of Democratic Action in Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MR. DE
utterances.text: But when Mr. Krzic asked you to count, to go to the cemetery at Seva regularly and to count the Serbian soldiers that had been buried there, didn't you think that this -- don't you think that this information -- do you think that this information had only a humanitarian objective?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAHUDIN SMAILAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, Mr. Krzic didn't tell me or order me to go to the cemetery to count bodies. And secondly, I think I said this yesterday, my house is in a street through which you have to pass to get to the new cemetery, and I've said this. Whenever you would pass by -- whenever they were transported, they were transported in refrigerators. You know, there was war propaganda and we always thought that this was an aggression against us, which it was. And we felt the moral obligation to inform our government of everything. Of all the events, whatever they concerned.

utterances.speaker: MR. DE
utterances.text: But the burial of Serbian soldiers was not an act of aggression against you.

utterances.speaker: ZIJAHUDIN SMAILAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. DE
utterances.text: I will ask that question again. It was more comment. In your opinion, where were these Serbian soldiers?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAHUDIN SMAILAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In various battlefields, I don't know which battlefields they were brought from but mainly from the battlefields.

utterances.speaker: MR. DE
utterances.text: Was the battlefield far away from Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAHUDIN SMAILAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were -- there was a lot of combat in the area of Travnik. There are several routes. I will try and tell you what the quickest route is. From Banja Luka to Travnik, it's about 90 kilometres and in the Bihacska and Krupska battlefield, that's about 160 or 150 kilometres away.

utterances.speaker: MR. DE
utterances.text: In the group that you frequented in Banja Luka, there weren't only members of the SDA, according to your statement, there were also members of a workers union. What sort of workers union was this?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAHUDIN SMAILAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were from almost all companies, the presidents of the unions, I didn't know about them but they had responded in 1991 when they were starting to dismiss people. They organised a well-known protest in Banja Luka under the auspices of the union and they fought for workers' rights. It wasn't until 1994 or at the end of 1993 that I saw one of them. One of them came to my place and that's how I met him.

utterances.speaker: MR. DE
utterances.text: That was Mr. Durakovic, I think, according to your statement. Was it Mr. Durakovic?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAHUDIN SMAILAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Durakovic. I met him in unfortunate conditions. On one occasion -- should I explain this?

utterances.speaker: MR. DE
utterances.text: Yes. Do tell us. On which occasion did you meet Mr. Durakovic?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAHUDIN SMAILAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On one occasion, while I was on the premises of the Merhamet organisation, one of those present asked me, since I had a larger house, whether I would receive Durakovic for one night, put him up for one night. Some unknown people had entered his house and beaten him. I accepted this. He spent about 15 or 20 days in my house, and then went to a third country.

utterances.speaker: MR. DE
utterances.text: On page 6 of the English version of your second statement, it's the paragraph before last, you say that Mr. Durakovic said that he had enough explosives to cause a great explosion in the city. What do you think of this statement that Mr. Durakovic made? In the Croatian version, I'll give you the -- it's page 7, the first paragraph, in the Serbo-Croatian version, page 7. At the top, after the first two lines, there you are. You have your finger on it.

utterances.speaker: ZIJAHUDIN SMAILAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was correct. Because, look, in Banja Luka, we were mostly engaged in this, that was to calm the situation and not to allow the population to provoke a conflict. Because explosives, hand grenades, weapons of any kind, all this was easily obtainable in Banja Luka. You could get it on the market from Serbian soldiers who would sell it. They were offering this. We did all we could to prevent this, to prevent weapons from being bought. We didn't want to die for nothing, because Banja Luka had no chances of any kind. And a second thing, he bought a pistol a rifle, or a bomb, in the afternoon, on the market. In the evening we came to the house and took this away. This was provocative. People wouldn't allow this to happen. It wasn't necessary. We always prevented such incidents from happening. And whether he had this or not, I'm not sure, these explosives.

utterances.speaker: MR. DE
utterances.text: But Mr. Durakovic said he had enough explosives to blow up the city. He asked you to put him up, he took refuge with you, took shelter with you. Do you think that this was an act of resistance on your part, an active act of resistance?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAHUDIN SMAILAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. DE
